issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

Jacob's hasty reaction to pull the child back resulted in a serious injury, leaving him paralyzed by guilt. The aftermath of that day haunted him relentlessly; he could still hear the echoes of the child's cries and see the look of sheer terror on their face. These vivid memories would often flood back with a jolt whenever he encountered certain triggers, such as seeing children playing in the park or hearing an ambulance siren, instantly transporting him to the scene of the accident. Each time he encountered reminders of that event, from the smell of antiseptic lingering in medical offices to the distant sirens of police cars, sharp waves of anxiety would wash over him, triggering a cascade of distressing thoughts and memories. In those moments, Jacob found himself increasingly drawn to filling his time with work tasks, believing that if he stayed busy, he could escape the grip of those overwhelming feelings that threatened to pull him under. In those moments, Jacob instinctively sought to fill his time with meetings and tasks at work, believing that staying busy would shield him from the overwhelming guilt and anxiety that surged at the thought of the accident. But this constant busyness only led to more triggers; he would find himself avoiding certain topics in meetings, fearing that any mention of safety protocols would remind him of the child's injury, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy. He would stay busy at work, filling his days with meetings and responsibilities, yet even in those moments, he could feel the faint tug of his trauma. During a school field trip, he had been responsible for supervising a group of children when one of them, distracted by a game, collided with a metal fence. Jacob's hasty reaction to pull the child back resulted in a serious injury, leaving him paralyzed by guilt. The aftermath of that day haunted him relentlessly; he could still hear the echoes of the child's cries and see the look of sheer terror on their face. These vivid memories would often flood back with a jolt whenever he encountered certain triggers, such as seeing children playing in the park or hearing an ambulance siren, instantly transporting him to the scene of the accident. Each time he encountered reminders of that event, from the smell of antiseptic lingering in medical offices to the distant sirens of police cars, sharp waves of anxiety would wash over him, triggering a cascade of distressing thoughts and memories. In those moments, Jacob instinctively sought to fill his time with meetings and tasks at work, believing that staying busy would shield him from the overwhelming guilt and anxiety that surged at the thought of the accident. In the months that followed, Jacob found himself employing various coping strategies to keep his mind occupied, avoiding any moments of stillness that might allow the horrific memory to surface. He would stay busy at work, filling his days with meetings and responsibilities, yet even in those moments, he could feel the faint tug of his trauma. The scent of antiseptic would take him back to the hospital where the child was treated, and he'd feel the panic rise in his chest. The panic triggered by these reminders often led Jacob to keep himself constantly busy at work, filling his days with meetings and responsibilities to avoid confronting the memories that threatened to surface. It was as if he had been thrust back into that moment, unable to find the words to articulate the depth of his sorrow and regret. Jacob's self-doubt morphed into an ever-present shadow, making him question his ability to make the right decisions. This deep-seated belief that he had made a grave mistake led him to avoid challenging situations, convinced that he would only prove his inadequacy again. His conviction that he was unworthy of making decisions often led him to avoid taking initiative, as he feared that any misstep would only reinforce his sense of failure. He felt as though his life had been irrevocably destroyed by that single moment of misjudgment. This pervasive sense of blame—believing that he had caused the injury because of his actions—only served to intensify his avoidance of the memories and situations associated with the accident. As he navigated his daily life, even the most innocuous encounters—a call from a parent or a discussion about student safety—would trigger a wave of anxiety, reminding him of his perceived failure and reinforcing his need to withdraw. He avoided places where he might run into police officers or area hospitals, as their presence could easily trigger another wave of guilt and anxiety. This avoidance became a map of his fear, with every location he bypassed reinforcing his belief that the world was filled with reminders of his failure and that confronting them was too dangerous to consider. He was terrified of the judgment he might face, both from the authorities and from himself, reinforcing a cycle of avoidance that left him feeling increasingly isolated.
